children.text:
That JS supports await isn't nearly as much a problem as the fact that it defensively defers execution any time it encounters one.

This hurts most badly for iterators.

Files are usually read from disks in chunks of 64K bytes. If you present the data as an async byte iterator you'll get 65,534 defensive deferrals, and one actual wait.

If you have ten layers of transformation it will be 655,350 defensive deferrals and 10 real waits.

These defensive deferrals aren't so expensive in terms of CPU time, but they ARE very expensive in terms of wall clock time. All other work must be halted so the event loop code can run. Eventually synthetic deferrals dominate the wall clock cost of running the program. This isn't hypothetical either. Here's someone trying to build steam parsing on Node and finding that it's too slow to be useful: https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/31979

The solution is stream iterators. They are sync when they can be and async when they must be: https://docs.bablr.org/architecture/spacetime

Yes, I keep saying this. Async await is like loading spinners - a fix for a problem that shouldn't exist in the first place.

As much as possible should be happening locally, synchronously on the computer, in-process, or at least without yielding your thread context (and even then there are things like page faults which async/await wont save you from, they are 'invisible' to a regular developer).

While you might dismiss this idea, page faults used to be THE leading cause of delays back when hard drives were the norm.

And a little research turns out that anthropic itself makes available a *react* based artifact builder so you don't end up with SLOP from the get go. You could probably modify the template to work with your framework of choice.

https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/skills/web-ar...

my experience is that one-shotting a simple front end works great. Then you want to add features and move things around and each turn starts getting slower and the single page with JS and CSS and HTML starts to turn into a 3000 line monster and your context window starts to creak under the strain of even simple changes, because the LLM has to keep more and more of the application in its head just to make relatively small changes without breaking something else. Either you should have started with some kind of framework with hygienic rules on how to separate concerns or at minimum a good set of coding standards that force the LLM to start building clean components from scratch. The benefit isn't necessarily cleaner code for its own sake, it's that the LLM can work on one part of the application without having to understand the whole thing every time. That being said, once you have a 3000 line prototype it's not that complex to simply ask the LLM to refactor it into a set of orthogonal components. As long as it was building unit tests using playwright or something this can turn your slop into framework code cleanly. The interesting question is whether you saved anything by putting off that structure in the first place.

No, nobody needs any more "experimental" Chrome bullshit.

The use case you mention, scrollable lists of static contents, works perfectly fine with DOM manipulation and virtualization, if you have a lot of content. Sure, maybe you can speed it up a bit with string manipulation (good luck not introducing XSS) but if you have so much content that this is a noticable factor, you probably want virtualization anyway.

It's astonishing to me that even after a decade of SPA frameworks, most authors don't understand how a browser engine like Chrome works. There's enormous cost of manipulating the DOM from JS, as HTML elements get bound to JS objects lazily.

An actual high performance framework should manipulate HTML as a string directly, or through HTML templates (another feature that has existed in most browsers for a decade).

If you're not building a complex application on top of the web stack (interestingly these increasingly use WASM and their own GUI frameworks, so another moot point), but building an interactive consumption website (scrollable lists of static contents), I'd say instead of fronted frameworks, what most people actually would need is Chrome's experimental declarative partial updates:

https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/declarative-p...

Which basically stream HTML fragments from the web.

This is true but its assessment did match my personal experience as a developer who has built quite a few apps with React + Node.js + Postgres combo. The project I had written with my framework was only about 1400 lines of code (mostly declarative HTML) and my experience is that applications of that complexity would normally approach or exceed 10k lines if well written with React/Node/Postgres. So its assessment even seemed conservative based on my own estimate.

I once also worked on a simpler application (feature-wise) for someone else which was approaching 100k lines but it was poorly architected with a lot of bad abstractions and over-engineered. In this case I could claim that my framework is cutting almost 99% of the code but that's comparing to the worst possible situation. Still, even that's not necessarily an unfair comparison because, in practice, a lot of real projects do end up bloated to such extent after a decade or so, likely even more so now with AI. Any framework which can prevent that bloat code from being generated is genuinely delivering long term benefits.
AI is notoriously bad at estimating length of tasks. Like humans.

I enjoyed reading this article. I think it's an important article. Even though people might disagree about certain definitions like "maintainability," I liked what the author did by sticking to objective measurements which do correlate somewhat with the things we care about: Ability to implement the product fast, with few tokens and with as few lines of code as possible in the final product. These are well chosen metrics IMO.

Fewer lines of code (per piece of functionality) does, in fact, correlate strongly with maintainability. The downside of this metric to watch out for (as Goodhart's Law would have it) is to ensure that the framework isn't compromising (current or future) flexibility in an unacceptable way. I imagine if this kind of benchmark becomes popular, people would start coming up with low code frameworks which are extremely rigid and inflexible. Because rigidity is a good way to cut lines of code. There needs to be a way to ascertain the flexibility limits of the framework too.

Would be good to have a similar benchmark for a more complex application; one with authentication, access control (with individual ownership of records and group ownership).

Also would be good to compare the security of different frameworks in this way. See which frameworks leave security gaps. Would be good to set up a benchmark where an AI agent is made to impersonate different users (with different roles) and test access to all possible data types and views in an exhaustive way.

A while ago, I showed Claude a relatively complex application I had built with my framework https://saasufy.com/ and asked it to estimate how many lines of code and how long would be required to build the same application with a stack like React + Node.js + Postgres and it estimated that it would require 4 to 5 times the amount of code and amount of time so I'm keen to actually test it out with a benchmark like this.

I was not surprised that HTMX lead in a lot of the benchmarks. I suspect it would do even better with a more complex application. IMO, its design is closer in spirit to where the industry needs to go. There are a lot of maintainability and security gains to be had by standardizing frontend and backend interactions; though I believe there are other way to do this which can yield even more gains (though obviously with some tradeoffs depending on the use case).

You're committing the very sin that the original article fingers as the problem with the webdev culture.

The evidence-free claim here (that with frameworks you end up spending less) is all "vibes"—or, put more charitably, a hunch plus some inductive reasoning. It's not a tested hypothesis.

The crux of your argument* is essentially "a + b > a for some non-zero b", where b represents what you are "paying for your library code". The right side of the relation is supposed to represent using a framework, but this neglects c, the cost paid for not using the Nike method ("Just Do It") when it comes to dealing with things yourself (i.e. the framework cost—which, like b, is never zero).

* as stated at least; it's possible and probable that you really don't mean to say that c simply doesn't exist but that b > c (either by intuition or experience or both) but that's still just a claim—which is the entire basis for the author's criticism: not whether frameworks are or aren't actually more cost-effective, but the greater meta-level concern described here in this comment, in the original piece, and other comments by the author and people like Alex Russell elsewhere describing how resistant the culture is towards the notion of attempting to prove or falsify these kinds of claims (if you can even manage to get people to agree to formulate them in such a way that they can actually be subjected to the scientific method)

children.text:
Unless the interactivity would have span page reload, there’s no need for SPA. Figma, Spotify and Google Docs are food candidates for SPA as they have state that need to survive page navigation.

But in most web apps, interactive widgets are just little islands in the page. The higher concerns are routing, authorization,… which are already handled by the browser/server interaction.

If you want an nice interactive interface SSR just won't do, it will inevitably leak. The separation between pure data and how that translates into UI through a wire interface is both natural and arguably desirable for many reasons. Typescript is a good language for UI. Java is a good language for backend. I disagree that evolving the API necessitates UI changes, or vice versa. You do need some amount of coordination of course, but if you can have developers do SSR, you can also have them do both SPA frontend and REST backend work - now more than ever.

A lot of times, most web app would be way better with purely server rendered pages. SPAs usually introduce a needless artificial separation. Too many times, I’ve seen an API that is tightly coupled with the web frontend instead of being agnostic and then starts being a maintenance nightmare because you have to coordinate across whole codebase because any Change Request updates the interface.

> If it were I suppose we would be seeing way less react and more vanilla with jquery on forms and normal website stuff.

The reason we moved away from this and into functional/reactive programming with things like React is that it eventually creates a mess too big to untangle. We made this experience with human developers and I made exactly the same experience with LLMs, trying to go "vanilla". It works for a while but the defect rate rises quickly und the LLM spends a large amount of time navigating the mess it created. I ended up with React again because it lets you express a lot of stuff as pure transforms, which are easy to reason about for human and LLM alike, and the LLM knows it very well out of the gate.

And by "React" I don't mean "react router" and all the other unstable crap in the ecosystem. React itself is stable and that is extremely important for LLMs, otherwise it will constantly conflate what the API actually looks like now. Breaking API changes are poison, worse than going with an in-house library that the LLM doesn't know how to use, because at least then it will look it up straight away, rather than messing it up (because it _thought_ it knew how it is supposed to work) and _then_ looking it up..

> so that employers do not have to invest in training developers.

This does not make sense to me. What do you classify as employer here? Front end frameworks are usually pushed by developers, not management. If it were I suppose we would be seeing way less react and more vanilla with jquery on forms and normal website stuff.

The push to create a SPA with react and other bollocks is purely pressure from implementers. There is not a day that I don't see devs that are more interested in making "beautiful code" and architecture despite the actual requirements they were trying to solve for. Ai is changing that, I hope for the better, but only time will tell.

The are some very real costs to JavaScript frameworks. These frameworks do not exist to empower developers. They exist to:

* so that employers do not have to invest in training developers.

* to ease candidate selection at hiring, which greases the wheels of hiring/firing

In the big corporate world, especially at non-software companies, there is a culture that strongly believes internally written software sucks. This is Invented Here syndrome, and it reflects that internal developers cannot write software and employers will not invest in maintenance.

The larger costs there are human costs, the inability to efficiently solve any problem outside the constraints imposed by the framework.
